main.text: It is proved that צפע tsepha, or צפעני tsiphoni, is the regulus, or basilisk.

Of the serpent צפע tsepha, or צפעני tsiphoni, we read in Prov. XXIII, 32. At the last it will bite like a serpent, and sting like tsiphoni. And Esa. XI, 8. The sucking child shall play over the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the den of tsiphoni. And Es. XIV, 29. Out of the serpent's root shall come forth tsepha. And Esa. LIX, 5. They hatch the eggs of tsiphoni, etc. He who eats of their eggs shall die; and if one crushes them, a viper will break out. And Ierem. VIII, 17. I will send among them serpents, tsiphonim, against which there is no charm; and they shall bite you, says the Lord. From these passages it is clear enough that these are very savage serpents. But to determine the species is not easy. The Greeks in some places render κεράστας [kerastas], in others ἀσπίδας [aspidas] and ἔγγονα ἀσπίδων [engona aspidōn], in others ὄφεις θανατοῦντας [opheis thanatountas]; the Chaldee consistently חורמנין hurmanim, as the Syriac mostly has ܚܘܪܡܢܝܢ hormanin, but once ܐܣܦܣ, asp, and once ܓܪܣܐ, amphisbaena. Aquila has βασιλίσκους [basiliskous], Jerome regulos, Münster hydros, Junius haemorrhoos, Castalio viperas. Kimchi says only that the serpent is הקשה והרע, harsh and evil, and Aquinas קשה ורע, harsh and dire.

We prefer Jerome's version to all of these. 1. Because among the ancients it has more supporters. For Aquila, by far the most accurate of all the translators, had led the way. To this is added the authority of the Chaldee paraphrast, who consistently renders חורמן hurman, as the Syriac mostly has ܚܘܪܡܢ horman, that is, the regulus; like the Arabic حرمانا [ḥrmānā] harmene, by which word, it is agreed, either the regulus or a serpent very similar to the regulus is meant. For Avicenna relates that the bite of both is incurable, and that both harm not only by their bite but also by their gaze and hiss. Thus, as he had said of the basilisk, تقتل بصفيرها الي علوة ومن وقع عليه بصرها من بعيد مات [taqtul bi-ṣafīrihā ilā ghalwa wa-man waqaʿa ʿalayhi baṣaruhā min baʿīd māt] It kills with its hiss [col. 400] as far as a bowshot (the translator ineptly has if it raises itself). And he on whom its gaze falls from afar dies; so he writes of the harmene in the following chapter: قد ذكر حرمانا في صفات قريبة من صفات الملكة من انها لا تسوي وليس انما تقتل باللسع فقط بل باللحظ وباسماع الصفير [qad dhukira ḥrmānā fī ṣifāt qarība min ṣifāt al-malika min annahā lā tusawwī wa-laysa innamā taqtul bi-l-lasʿ faqaṭ bal bi-l-laḥẓ wa-bi-ismāʿ al-ṣafīr] It is indeed recorded that the harmene has attributes very close to the attributes of the basilisk, since it injures, or indeed kills, not by its bite alone, [III, 183] but also by its gaze and by the hearing of its hiss. Hence the Pandectarius: Harmene, basilisk. Likewise: Karmene (wrongly for Harmene) is a serpent that kills not only by its bite but by its gaze and by being heard, that is, by its hiss. Avicenna holds that they differ only in size, since the length of the basilisk is said to be شبران الي ثلثة [shibrān ilā thalātha] from two spans to three, but that of the harmene من ذراع الي ذراع ونصف [min dhirāʿ ilā dhirāʿ wa-niṣf] from one cubit to a cubit and a half. But here he has overlooked the relation of the measures. For شبر [shibr] is the greater span, in Greek σπιθαμὴ [spithamē], a measure of twelve fingers, which doubled makes a cubit. So a length of two to three spans is exactly the same as one of one to one and a half cubits. These two measures differ in words but agree in substance. Other Arabs, however, more correctly assign the basilisk only one شبر [shibr], that is, one σπιθαμὴν [spithamēn] of length. Alkazuinius in the chapter حية [ḥayya], or On Serpents: ومنها الحية تقال لها الملكة طولها شبرا واكثر [wa-minhā al-ḥayya tuqāl lahā al-malika ṭūluhā shibran wa-akthar] Among them also is the serpent Almelecha (or basilisk), whose length is a span (the greater) and more. So also Damir in the chapter الملكة [al-malika] Almelecha. Most of the ancients report what agrees with this. Nicander, Theriaca, verse 398.
Ξανθὸς, ἐπὶ τρία δῶρα φέρων μῆκός τε, καὶ ἰθὺν. [Xanthos, epi tria dōra pherōn mēkos te, kai ithyn.]

It is yellow, about three (lesser) palms in length, and has a (growing) impetus. These three lesser palms make one greater palm, that is, one σπιθαμή [spithamē]; for each is of four fingers. Aelian, History book 2, ch. 5: Σπιθαμὴ δὲ τοῦ βασιλίσκου τὸ μῆκός ἐστι [Spithamē de tou basiliskou to mēkos esti]; The length of the basilisk is one spithame, or greater palm. Pliny book 8, ch. 21: The province of Cyrenaica produces it, no more than twelve fingers in size. Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 1, ch. 33: This animal is three palms in size; in Greek, if I am not mistaken, τριῶν παλαιστῶν [triōn palaistōn]. This is the true size of the basilisk, which was tripled by those who assigned it a cubit and a half, or three σπιθαμάς [spithamas], confusing the greater palms with the lesser; writers warn that this happens frequently. Further, why it is called חורמן hurman by the Chaldeans, R. Selomo explains in these words on Genes. XLIX, 17.: חורמן שם מין נחש שאין רפואה לנשיכתו והוא צפעני וקרוי חורמן על שם שעושה הכל חרם, Hurman is the name of a species of serpent whose bite is incurable. It is TSIPHONI to the Hebrews, and in Chaldee is called HURMAN, because it makes everything חרם, a devastation: that is, because it destroys and lays waste all things and annihilates them.

Second, the Hebrew name צפע tsepha, or צפעני tsiphoni, fits the basilisk [col. 401] exceedingly well, because by its very sound it seems to express the horror of the hiss with which it either puts the other animals to flight or kills them. The older writers had said only that it puts them to flight. Nicander, in the place cited above, [III, 184] Οὐκ ἄρα δὴ κείνου σπειραχθέα κνώδαλα γαίης Ἰϋγὴν μίμνουσιν [Ouk ara dē keinou speirachthea knōdala gaiēs Iygēn mimnousin], etc.

The reptiles of the earth, laden with coils (of the tail) (that is, the larger ones), do not await its hiss. Archelaus in Aelian, book 2, chapter 7: Ἐπὰν δὲ βασιλίσκου συρίγματος ἀκούσῃ, (τὰ τῶν ὄφεων φῦλα) τὰ μὲν ὑπὸ τοῖς ἰλεοῖς, καὶ τῇ ψάμμῳ, ἀφανίζεσθαι τὴν ταχίστην [Epan de basiliskou syrigmatos akousē, (ta tōn opheōn phyla) ta men hypo tois ileois, kai tē psammō, aphanizesthai tēn tachistēn]; When they have heard the hiss of the regulus (the kinds of snakes) at once hide themselves in holes or under the sand, etc. Lucan, book 9:
And pouring forth hisses that terrify all the pests.

Pliny: With its hiss it puts all serpents to flight. Solinus: Even other serpents shudder at its hiss. But later writers assert that the basilisk's hiss is deadly. Galen, chapter 8 of To Piso: Ὁρασθεὶς μόνον, καὶ συρίττων ἀκουσθεὶς, ἀναιρεῖ τοὺς ἀκούσαντας, καὶ τοὺς ἰδόντας αὐτόν [Horastheis monon, kai syrittōn akoustheis, anairei tous akousantas, kai tous idontas auton]; Merely by being seen, and heard when it hisses, it kills those who hear and see it. Aëtius: They say that, heard hissing, it carries off those who have heard it. Damir, where he treats Of the species of serpents: ونوع اخر اذا سمع الانسان صغيره مات [wa-nawʿ ākhar idhā samiʿa al-insān ṣaghīrahu māta] There is another species of serpent: whoever hears its hiss dies. And Alkazuinius: اذا صغرت تموت من صغيرها كل حيوان سمع ذلك بعد ما ينفخ ويسيل منه الصديد [idhā ṣaghirat tamūtu min ṣaghīrihā kull ḥayawān samiʿa dhālika baʿda mā yanfukhu wa-yasīlu minhu al-ṣadīd], When it hisses, on hearing its hiss all animals die, as soon as it has blown and released its poison. Add to these what has already been cited from Avicenna. But note especially this passage of Isidore: The SIBILUS is the same as the regulus; for it kills by its hiss before it either bites or burns. Thus, just as in Latin sibilus comes from sibilo [to hiss], so in Hebrew it could be called TSEPHA or TSIPHONI from the sound it makes while hissing.

Third, the Arabic verb سفع [safaʿa] saphaa, which means to scorch with a blast, seems to allude to the Hebrew צפע tsepha. Hence καύσωνες [kausōnes], scorching winds, are called سوافع [sawāfiʿ] ^{(1)}. For this is precisely the property of the basilisk: it scorches with its breath. Horapollo, book 1 [III, 185] of the Hieroglyphica, chapter 1: Προσφυσῆσαν ἑτέρῳ παντὶ ζώῳ (τοῦτο γένος,) δίχα καὶ τοῦ δακεῖν ἀναιρεῖ [Prosphysēsan heterō panti zōō (touto genos,) dicha kai tou dakein anairei]; This kind, if it has breathed upon any other animal, kills it even without a bite. And book 2, chapter 57: Τοὺς πλησιάζοντας τῷ ἑαυτοῦ φησήματι φονεύει [Tous plēsiazontas tō heautou phēsēmati phoneuei]; It kills those who approach with its breath. Aelian, Historia book 2, ch. 5: Θεασάμενος ὁ τῶν ὄφεων μήκιστος αὐτὸν, οὐκ εἰς ἀναβολὰς, ἀλλ᾽ ἤδη ἐκ τῆς τοῦ φυσήματος προσβολῆς αὐτός ἐστιν [Theasamenos ho tōn opheōn mēkistos auton, ouk eis anabolas, all᾽ ēdē ek tēs tou physēmatos prosbolēs autos estin] (read καυτὸς [kautos], or καυστός ἐστιν [kaustos estin]). A serpent, one of the very largest, on seeing it, is burnt up not after some delay but at once by the force of its breath. Pliny, book 8, chapter 21: It kills shrubs, not only those it touches but also those it breathes upon; it scorches grasses, it bursts rocks: such is the power of this evil creature. Solinus: It extinguishes grasses, kills trees, and corrupts even the very air. Therefore, just as the basilisk is called צפע tsepha, so سفع [safaʿa] saphaa, said of the wind, means to burn and to scorch, as the basilisk does, in whose breath there is a caustic power. The former, indeed, is written with Tsade, the latter with Sin. But among the Arabs the letters Sin and Sad or Sade are so interchangeable that they write countless words with either. Thus سلط [sallaṭa] or صلط [ṣallaṭa], he set in authority; اسلنطح [islanṭaḥa] or اصلنطح [iṣlanṭaḥa], it was broad; سوق [sūq] or صوق [ṣūq], street; [col. 402] سراط [sirāṭ] or صراط [ṣirāṭ], way, if written with Kesre, and long sword, if with Damma; سقاب [siqāb] or صقاب [ṣiqāb], a bloodied fillet, which Arab women wear when they have met with some grievous misfortune; سنط [sanṭ] or صنط [ṣanṭ], acacia; سعطر [saʿtar] or صعطر [ṣaʿtar], origanum; اسفنط [isfanṭ] or اصفنط [iṣfanṭ], a kind of drink made from grape juice seasoned with spices; سعوط [saʿūṭ] or صعوط [ṣaʿūṭ], an ἔῤῥινον [errhinon] for purging the head; مسمرط [musamraṭ] or مصمرط [muṣamraṭ], oblong of head, etc. ^{(2)}.

[III, 186] Fourth, even if there was no basilisk in Judaea, it could nevertheless have been known to the Jews through the Egyptians. For it was common in Egypt, and in Libya and Cyrenaica, which border on Egypt. Ammianus, book 22: Egypt also nourishes innumerable serpents, raging beyond all destructiveness: basilisks and amphisbaenas, etc. Pliny, book 8, chapter 21: The province of Cyrenaica produces it. Solinus: Behind Cyrene lie various barbarian nations, and an uncultivated wilderness, squalid and inaccessible, which breeds the basilisk. Aelian, book 3, chapter 31, calls Libya τὴν τῶν τοιούτων τροφὸν [tēn tōn toioutōn trophon], the land that nurtures such creatures. And Avicenna says it abounds ببلاد الترك ولوبية [bi-bilād al-Turk wa-Lūbiya] in the region of Turkey and Libya, not of Arorch and Nubia, as the translators have it. Thus the basilisk was very well known to the Egyptians, who in their language called it ΟΥΒΑΙ͂ΟΝ [ouBAION] (just as even today they call any serpent ʼΟΒΙῸΝ [obion]), and they placed a golden basilisk around the heads of the gods. And in their symbols they signified a sycophant by the basilisk, which kills by its breath alone, just as they signified eternity by the image of a basilisk hiding its tail beneath the rest of its body. See Horapollo, book 1, chapter 1, and book 2, chapter 57.

notes.text: ومنه لنسفعن بالناصية سفع الطاير لطم اي لنجرنه بها الي النار بجناحية وفلان فلانا او لنسودن وجهه او لنعلمنه لطمه وضربه والشي اعلمه علامة اهل النار والسوافع ووسمه والسموم وجهه لفحه لوايح السموم لفحا يسيرا وبناصيته قبض عليها فاجتذ بها [wa-minhu la-nasfaʿanna bi-l-nāṣiya safaʿa al-ṭāyir laṭama ay la-najurrannahu bihā ilā al-nār bi-janāḥiyya wa-fulān fulānan aw la-nusawwidanna wajhahu aw la-nuʿlimannahu laṭamahu wa-ḍarabahu wa-l-shay aʿlamahu ʿalāmat ahl al-nār wa-l-sawāfiʿ wa-wasamahu wa-l-samūm wajhahu lafaḥahu lawāyiḥ al-samūm lafḥan yasīran wa-bi-nāṣiyatihi qabaḍa ʿalayhā fa-ijtadha bihā]. The verb سفع [safaʿa], said of a bird, means: it clapped its wings; it also means: it struck with a sound; [III, 185] and further: it struck with a resounding blow. Also: it branded something with a mark. A pestilential wind is also said to clap, to strike, someone's face, when it scorches him with its heat by a mere blast or touch. Also, with "by the forelocks", it means to seize and drag; as in that passage of the Qur'an (Sur. 96: 15.): truly We shall clap their faces by the forelocks, that is, We shall seize them by the forelocks and drag them to the fire of Gehenna; or, We shall blacken their faces, or brand them with the mark of the damned in the fire. Finally, the winds that scorch and blacken with a pestilential blast are called the clappers (which strike with a hiss). So FIRUZABADI, in Schultens on Proverb. XXIII, 30. p. 305.

Bochart could have added that the root صفع [ṣafaʿa] is also preserved in the Arabic dialect, and that it has the same meaning as سفع [safaʿa], namely to blow upon, to strike with a blast or with a hiss. Thus Amr ibn Kulthum in the Muʿallaqa, describing triple-meshed coats of mail: كان غضونهن متون عدر تصفعها الرياح اذا جرينا [ka-anna ghuḍūnahunna mutūnu ghudrin taṣfaʿuhā al-riyāḥu idhā jarayna] As if their wrinkles were the surfaces of pools which the winds ruffle with their blast when we are urged on at a run. [III, 186] So Schultens, loc. cit. It is clear that the two roots, سفع [safaʿa] and صفع [ṣafaʿa], agree with each other not only in sound but also in meaning, since the first notion of both, to strike, to hit, is transferred first to the burning wind called Samum, when it touches or strikes someone's face with its heat, and then to any burning and harmful blast, such as is attributed to basilisks, which for this reason received the name צפע among the Hebrews. — According to Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 6, p. 2130, the basilisk seems to have received the name צפע from صُوفَعَة [ṣūfaʿa] turban; "for," he says, "it bore something on its head, which the Greeks called horns and so named it κεράτην [keratēn]; others compared it to a crown or diadem and called it regulus, βασιλισκον [basiliskon], recognizing it as the king, as it were, and the most powerful of serpents."
